analysis.investment_thesis: Blue Dart earns a borderline earnings yield of ~6.4% but pairs it with a mediocre and declining ROCE of 16.3% — net profit has fallen four consecutive years from the FY2022 peak of INR 382 Cr to INR 252 Cr. Greenblatt's formula needs both metrics to be high; a deteriorating earnings base with moderate returns does not qualify.
key_strengths: Strong brand with premium logistics positioning and DHL network backing — genuine intangible moat
Consistent OCF generation (5/5 years positive, INR 735 Cr in FY2025) — business does produce cash
Revenue CAGR of 9.3% and a domestic air-express monopoly provide a degree of pricing power
key_risks: Net profit declining for four straight years (INR 382 → 371 → 301 → 252 Cr) — earnings deterioration destroys Magic Formula attractiveness
EBITDA trend described as 'contracting' — rising competition from Delhivery and quick-commerce logistics eroding margins
INR 1,008 Cr in debt (predominantly Ind AS 116 lease liabilities for aircraft/hubs) adds fixed cost burden; EBIT materially lower than EBITDA
red_flags: Net profit CAGR of only 2.8% over 9 years — poor compounding for a stock at 44x P/E
EBITDA trend is contracting — the headline metric looks okay but the direction is wrong
75% owned by DHL Singapore — minority shareholders' interests may not always be prioritized in capital allocation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Blue Dart is India's premium express logistics leader with genuine brand advantages and the backing of Deutsche Post DHL. But the Magic Formula is indifferent to brand quality if earnings are declining. Net profit peaked at INR 382 Cr in FY2022 and has fallen every year since to INR 252 Cr — a 34% decline in absolute profit while revenue grew 30%. This margin compression signals structural cost pressure: aircraft lease costs, fuel, labor, and competitive price undercutting from Delhivery and Zomato/Swiggy dark-store fulfillment are real forces.

ROCE of 16.3% is adequate but not exciting — and it is likely overstated because Ind AS 116 lease accounting inflates 'assets' relative to old treatment. The true return on tangible capital deployed in aircraft and logistics hubs is lower. At P/E of 44x on a declining earnings base, the forward P/E of 28x is only 'better' if you believe the profit decline has bottomed. That is a hope trade, not a Magic Formula trade.
